At a hold, play() and toggle() release it seek(t)jump to t seconds (clamped between the first scene's negative time, or 0, and total) jumpScene(d)go to the start of the scene d steps away next(), prev()→ and ←: next() releases a hold (and plays on), otherwise it is jumpScene(1) release()let a hold go: the next scene starts and playback continues. false when nothing was holding reset()stop, clear a hold and rewind to start (default 0) advance(dt)per frame; moves t by dt × rate while playing state(t), valueAt(key, t)the automation values at a time (no overrides) sceneIndexAt(t), currentScene(t), sceneEnd(i)scene lookup onSceneChange(cb)cb(index, scene, { cause }) whenever playback or a seek lands in a different scene; cause is 'play', 'release', 'seek', 'jump', 'reset' or 'loop' onCue(cb), cues(), fireCue(cue)scene cues fired by playback, the list of them, and the manual trigger loop, onLoop(cb), loopRange(), loopswrap the show, a scene or a range record(key, source), stopRecording(), onRecord(cb), mergeTake(key, take)write a value source into a lane onSeek(cb)cb(t, kind) when the playhead is moved by hand ('seek', 'jump', 'reset'), never while playing layer(key, value, t) => value: rewrite a param before overrides (the director's param() plugs in here) t, playing, holding, rate, total, start, scenes, automation, scorestate you can read (and set)

Curves. A keyframe is [t, value, curve?]. The third item says how the segment that ends at that keyframe gets there: 'linear' (the default: leave it out and you get what the timeline always did), 'ease' (slow, fast, slow), 'in' (starts slow), 'out' (starts fast), 'step' (hold the old value until the keyframe, then jump), or your own function of 0..1. CURVES is exported. A param with step still holds, whatever the curve says. jsCopy Loop. loop: true wraps at total (back to 0) and keeps playing; 'scene' repeats the scene the playhead is in (next() moves the loop on to the next scene); a scene id loops that scene; { from, to } loops a range in seconds or scene ids. It is a property: timeline.loop = !timeline.loop is the whole L key. onLoop(cb) tells you each lap, and a loop that wraps into another scene is an onSceneChange with cause: 'loop'. A hold inside the range still holds. Cues. scene.cues is [{ name, t }] (the console scrubber already draws them as ticks). onCue((cue, { cause }) => …) fires one when playback passes it, once, and never when you seek, jump, drag the scrubber or reset: a scrub is not a performance. Each lap of a loop fires them again. fireCue(cue) sets one off by hand. With a score the director fires its own cues; use onCue on plain timelines. jsCopy Recording. record(key, source) arms a lane. While the timeline plays, source() is read every frame: a number is written into a take, null means nobody is touching and closes it. jsCopy A take also closes on pause, seek, reset, a hold, the end of the show and the end of each loop lap, while the recorder stays armed until stop() / stopRecording(). The merge rule (mergeTake()): the take is thinned (a point stays when it moved more than 0.6 % of the param's range, or 0.5 s passed), and it replaces the keyframes inside its time span. Keyframes outside stay, so the lane glides from the previous keyframe to the take's first point, and from its last point to the next keyframe. Existing curves outside the take are untouched. With a score the keyframes are written in the base cut's time, like the ones you declared. A cue list is just a scene-change handler: jsCopy

mountConsole(el, app, { layers, signals }) (@openav/console) builds the director's desk; createShow() mounts it in the side panel. app is the object createShow() returns as show.app (timeline, params, mapper, signals, stage, midi, sound, audio, hands, pose, …); missing parts simply hide their section. Pass { layers: false } or { signals: false } to leave out those panels. It gives you transport + scrubber with scene blocks, the Layers overview, L1 Input, L2 Mapping, L3 Params (sliders with override and learn chips), L4 sound, live signal meters and a MIDI log. Keyboard: Space play/pause (at a hold: release) · →/← next / previous scene (→ at a hold: release) · R reset · T performance mode · F fullscreen · Esc leave keyboard-piano capture or stop the mapping wizard. Keys typed into an input field, held keys and ⌘/Ctrl/Alt combinations are ignored. While the on-screen piano captures the keyboard the letters belong to the piano (T and F are piano keys), so R, T and F do nothing until you untick it or press Esc; Space and the arrows always work. With a score the desk also has the Director panel, cue ticks on the scrubber and a prompter with the operator's acts (Score & Director). The L2 Mapping panel has 🎛 map knobs in order, a wizard that arms learn for each param in turn (details). Override semantics: touch a slider (or a mapped control) and that param leaves the timeline's hands until you clear it (✕). Yellow label = overridden.

T flips to a fullscreen teleprompter: current scene title + note in stage- readable type, what the operator does (the scene's acts), next scene preview, clock + scene countdown, a HOLD banner while the show waits, and a warning when a segment module was switched off. This is for the performer; the audience-facing window is your stage in fullscreen (F). Two windows of the same page = one desk, one stage.

bashCopy Every show page made with createShow() streams snapshots to ws://<the page's host>:7457 about 15 times a second, so run the monitor server on the machine that serves the show. Backstage shows clock, scene, world, FPS, overrides, all signals and params live, and a red "stage feed lost" banner if the stage stops sending for 4 s — which is exactly the moment a stage manager earns their pay. Zero configuration, zero dependencies; both ends reconnect by themselves. GET /health answers { ok, clients }. When no monitor is running, the show page keeps retrying with a growing delay (about 5 s, growing to 30 s); the browser logs each refused connection. That message is expected. For a hand-assembled show: jsCopy

bashCopy The defaults are 7456 127.0.0.1 3456. The browser cannot send UDP, so OscOut posts batches to the bridge over HTTP and the bridge sends them as OSC packets. jsCopy Numbers go out as OSC floats — what Spat, Reaper, and TouchDesigner expect; anything else is sent as a string. Only the latest message per address survives a frame. If the bridge disappears, OscOut reports it through onStatus(ok, info) and stops trying after 30 failed flushes. createShow() does not create an OscOut. Add one yourself (and add "@openav/osc": "../../packages/osc/index.js" to the page's import map): jsCopy

OSC goes to TouchDesigner as above. TouchDesigner can also show an open-audiovisual page as a picture with its Web Render TOP, which draws a web page inside TouchDesigner on the same machine (Web Render TOP). We have not checked whether the Web Render TOP supports Web MIDI or WebGPU. Keep the control on OSC. If the page comes from openaudiovisual.com, Chrome asks before the page may reach the bridge on 127.0.0.1: see Chrome asks about the local network (Chrome blog). Running node serve.js and opening the page from http://localhost:8080 avoids the prompt.

midi.noteOn/noteOff/cc/send go to the selected output port — and midi.panic() sends all-notes-off + all-sound-off + sustain-off + per-note note-offs on all 16 channels, through the same observable throat as everything else. Bind it to a pad you can find in the dark. Every performer eventually needs it; ours is one call. jsCopy The first output port is used until you choose another (enable(preferredOut) matches a name exactly, then as a substring). Everything sent passes through onSend, which feeds the per-channel MIDI OUT meter in the Layers panel. Hot-plug. A cable pulled mid-show must not leave the DAW silent without a word. When the current output is unplugged, Midi moves to the next best live port: the one you chose with selectOutput() or enable(name), then the first match of the prefer list (new Midi({ prefer: ['IAC'] })), then the first port. When the port you chose is plugged in again, the output goes back to it. An unrelated device appearing never steals the output. Every switch prints one line in the MIDI log (the Signals panel, via midi.onMessage) and one in the browser console, flashes in the MIDI controller panel, and updates the MIDI out → row of the L1 Input panel. In code: midi.onOutput(({ text, reason }) => …). Echo. What you send into a virtual bus must not come back as input. Inputs whose name matches filterOut (default IAC, the macOS bus) are never listened to, and a message identical to one just sent that arrives on any input within echoWindow milliseconds (default 40; 0 turns it off) is dropped as echo, once per message sent. midi.echoDropped counts them. To make an external program follow the show, ScoreMidi sends the score's segment changes and cues as notes and CCs (Score to MIDI).

modules: { sound: true } adds Sound (@openav/sound) with the Tone.js engine. Browsers only start audio after a click, so the console shows 🔊 enable sound in the L4 · Output — sound panel, with an instrument picker under it. Once enabled, every midi/note/on and midi/note/off plays the chosen instrument, whatever sent it (a keyboard, the QWERTY piano, the simulated performer, a phone). Tone.js (15.0.4) is loaded from jsDelivr only when sound is enabled. jsCopy

If they cannot load, the piano plays the electric piano instead of going silent.

Pick from the console, or from code: jsCopy Switching while you play releases the notes held on the old instrument, so nothing hangs. A sampler keeps the old sound playing until its files are in, and the picker shows the progress. Each switch also fires the pulse signal sound/instrument ({ id, name }). The picker's last choice is remembered per page and wins over the declared instrument on the next visit; remember: false turns that off. The instrument is a discrete choice. What you perform continuously stays a param: the engine's params join the show's params under sound/. sound/cutoff (100–8000 Hz, default 2500), sound/space (reverb wet, 0–1, default 0.3) and sound/volume (−36–0 dB, default −8) are shared by every instrument, so a knob, a hand or the score plays the filter the way it plays the visuals. An instrument may suggest starting values (the piano opens the filter to 8000 Hz) and add knobs of its own, which the console shows while it plays: the organ's sound/drawbars and sound/rotor, sound/attack and sound/vibrato on the strings, sound/vowel on the choir, sound/tremolo on the electric piano and the vibraphone. Automation and overrides always win over a suggested default. The sustain pedal (midi/cc/64) holds every instrument's note-offs. Notes on MIDI channel 10 (the drum machine) are left to a drum engine.

A sound you can pick is one file: data plus a create(Tone, ctx) that returns noteOn, noteOff and dispose. Import it before createShow() and every picker lists it; nothing in packages/* changes. jsCopy A duplicate id throws unless you pass registerInstrument(def, { replace: true }). Optional fields: defaults (starting cutoff, space, volume), credit, gain (dB), transpose (semitones), fallback (an id to play if loading fails) and, on the returned object, ready (a Promise: the picker shows progress while you call ctx.onProgress(0..1)), set(key, value) and releaseAll(time). Mallet sounds can be pure data with modalInstrument({ id, name, partials, strike }). A synth preset is data as well, and becomes synth/<id>: jsCopy

An engine is a small object, so you can replace the whole thing: jsCopy The drum kit from @openav/drums is also an engine: drumEngine({ samples }) maps General MIDI drum notes to synthesized drums (or to your samples, { 36: 'kick.wav', … }) and has one param, kitVolume (−30–0 dB).
createShow() is a convenience. When you need your own layout or loop, assemble the parts by hand; this is roughly what it does: jsCopy

Chrome, plugged in, screen-sleep off, notifications off (chrome://settings) WebMIDI permission granted for this origin (it's per-origin, per-port) mapping profile saved (mapper.save()) AND exported to a JSON file monitor server running; stage manager's device on the same network sound enabled with a click, and the panic pad mapped rehearse the failure: kill the tab, restart, be performing again in <30 s

A show that outgrows one afternoon needs a structure that can grow. The score (@openav/score) writes a show down as segments with lengths, and the director runs the code that performs each segment. They are pure logic with no DOM, and createShow() wires them to the timeline, the console and the prompter for you.

A timeline written as a table of absolute seconds cannot grow. Make the second scene longer and every later scene, cue, curve and if (t > 466) in your code is now wrong, and you find them one rehearsal at a time. In a score you write only how long each segment is: jsCopy Every start, end, cue time, countdown and scene is computed from those lengths. Change noon to dur: 40 and everything after it moves by ten seconds while everything before it stays put. A second version of the show is a few lines of data, not a second timeline to keep in step.

A cut is one version of the show. It has an id, an optional title, and either segments or a base cut and a scale. cut fieldmeaning idunique among the cuts; no . titleshown in the cut picker segmentsthe list below, in playing order from, scalea derived cut: the cut named from with every length times scale (scale > 0). It can be derived again; the scales multiply startthe id of the segment the show opens on and reset returns to (default: the first) segment fieldmeaning idunique within the cut; no .. It is also the id of the module that performs it title, notewhat the desk and the prompter show durlength in seconds, greater than 0. The only time a segment has cuesnamed moments inside the segment: a ratio 0 ≤ r < 1 (a fraction of the segment) or { s: seconds } (seconds into it) actswhat the human operator does in this segment: an array of strings, shown on the desk and, large, on the prompter lingerseconds the segment's module keeps running after the segment ends (a decay, a tail). Default 0 holdplayback stops at the end of this segment and waits for the operator (Hold) modulethe name of the module that performs it, when that is not the segment's own id A derived cut scales dur, linger and { s } cues, so a cue stays in the same place in the music. The ratio cues did not need to move. A cut is checked when the score is built. Duplicate ids, a dur of 0 or below, a from that is not a cut, a scale of 0 or below, a cut derived from itself, a cue outside its segment, acts that are not strings: each throws a ScoreError that names the cut, the segment and the reason, and lists every problem at once. Nothing half-valid can reach the stage.

jsCopy memberwhat it gives table()one row per segment: { index, id, title, start, end, dur, linger, hold } totalthe show's length: the sum of the segment lengths segmentAt(T), indexAt(T)the segment playing at show time T. A segment owns [start, end); before 0 answers the first, after the end the last cueTime('dusk')a moment in show seconds: 'dusk' is the segment's start, 'dusk.end' its end, 'dusk.glow' a cue. NaN for anything unknown cuesBetween(T0, T1)the cues a playhead passed from T0 to T1: those with T0 < time ≤ T1, in time order. Nothing when T1 ≤ T0 cues()every cue of the cut in time order, each with its number n scenes()the segments as a scenes array for the timeline (with acts, hold and cues) validate()throws a ScoreError when anything is wrong; returns true otherwise (the constructor already calls it) cut, title, segments, startTthe active cut, and where reset goes cutsevery cut as { id, title, total, from, scale, base }, for a version picker scale, base, baseTime(T)the cut's total scale against the cut it was derived from, that cut's id, and T expressed on it

Automation curves are written once, against the cut they were derived from, and a derived cut stretches them. timeline.valueAt(key, t) reads the curve at score.baseTime(t), which is t / scale. On the short cut above, t = 20 reads the curve at 40. A cut that is not derived has scale 1 and nothing changes. If two cuts differ in structure and not just in length, do not share automation between them. Drive the params from the segment modules instead (param()), where ctx.p already scales for free.

A cue is a named moment: cues: { peak: 0.5 } in segment noon makes noon.peak, half way through. Three places see it: the scrubber draws a tick for it, and a click on the tick jumps there; the director calls onCue({ name, cue, T, n, segment }) once each time the playhead passes it while playing, and calls the active module's cue(name, ctx) hook; ctx.cue('peak') inside a module tells you where it sits, as a progress you can compare with ctx.p ('noon.peak' works for another segment's cue, ctx.cueT(name) answers in show seconds). A seek does not pass the cues it jumps over, and playing back over a cue fires it again. A cue sitting exactly on the first instant of the show fires on the first frame.

hold: true means: when playback reaches the end of this segment, stop and wait. A standby that waits for the room to be ready is the typical use. Exactly what happens: The timeline stops a microsecond before the boundary, so the show is still inside the held segment, and sets timeline.holding = true and timeline.playing = false. The clock freezes there for as long as you like. The held segment's module keeps getting update() every frame, with ctx.p === 1, ctx.holding === true and ctx.held, the number of seconds waited so far. Use ctx.held as the clock for anything that should keep breathing while the show is frozen. (This is the choice made: the show stops at the end of the segment rather than looping inside it. Looping would send p back to 0, fire the cues again and break "every module enters once, exits once".) Space, →, the ▶ button, timeline.play() and timeline.next() all release it: the next segment starts at once and playback continues. timeline.release() does the same in code. A seek (scrubber, goto, ←) or a reset clears the hold, and a seek never stops at a hold: only playback does. The last segment never holds (the show ends there). The backstage monitor shows ⏸ HOLD; the desk and the prompter show a pulsing banner.

A segment module is the code that performs one segment. Its id is the id of the segment (or the segment's module name): jsCopy enter, update and exit get the api object first (yours, see below). Every hook gets a ctx: ctxmeaning pprogress through the segment, 0 to 1. Above 1 during linger; exactly 1 while holding tseconds into the segment (p × dur) dtseconds since the previous frame durthe segment's length in seconds Tshow time in seconds segmentthe segment: id, title, start, end, dur, cues, acts, hold, linger, index cue(name), cueT(name)where a cue sits, as a progress and in show seconds (NaN when unknown) phase'active', 'linger', or 'failed' (only inside exit() after a crash) holding, heldwaiting at a hold, and for how many seconds playingwhether the timeline is running (update is called every frame regardless) apithe same api object, so param() and cue() can reach the show too Enter once, exit once. The module of a segment is entered when the show enters it and exited when it leaves it, however it got there. A seek into the middle of a segment calls enter with the right p, so the module must be able to start from the middle. linger. After the segment ends its module keeps getting update() (with p > 1 and phase: 'linger') until the linger is over, and only then exit(). The next segment's module is already running meanwhile. param(). While a segment (or its linger) is current its module may rewrite any timeline param. Return a number to replace the value, anything else leaves it. The performer's hand still wins: an override is applied after this layer. A module that throws is switched off, alone. Each hook runs inside its own try/catch. If one throws, the director calls that module's exit() once (with phase: 'failed'), prints one console.error, and never calls it again. The other modules and the show carry on. The desk shows a red warning with the module's name and the error; R (reset) switches it back on. A frame loop is not allowed to stop because the youngest code in the room failed.

With a score the console adds: Scrubber. Segment blocks, a tick for every cue (click to jump) and a dashed end on a segment that holds. Director panel. A cut picker (choosing one reloads the page with ?cut=<id>, so nothing is half-switched), the current segment with a progress bar and the time left, the HOLD banner, the next segment and the countdown, the operator's acts, this segment's cues (ticked as they pass), and the red warning for modules that were switched off. Prompter (T). Fullscreen, large, high-contrast: the segment title, what you do (acts), seconds left, the next segment, a HOLD banner while the show waits, and a red line for switched-off modules. Click it or press T again to leave. It also works for plain timeline scenes that carry acts.

keydoes Spaceplay / pause. At a HOLD: release it →next segment. At a HOLD: release it ←previous segment Rback to the start; stopped; switched-off modules come back Tprompter Ffullscreen Escstop the knob-mapping wizard, or leave keyboard-piano capture Typing in a field, a held key (auto-repeat) and any key with ⌘, Ctrl or Alt are ignored. While the on-screen piano captures the keyboard (the keyboard box ticked in the piano bar) the letters belong to the piano: R, T and F do nothing, because T and F are piano keys, and an accidental R must not rewind a show you are playing. Space, the arrows and Esc always work, so you can play and run the show from one keyboard. The MIDI-controller key M follows the same rule.

The L2 Mapping panel has 🎛 map knobs in order. It arms learn for the first param, you turn one knob, it is bound and the next param is armed; skip, back and stop (or Esc) steer it. Learn only ever adds routes (Mapper.learn), so running it again puts a second knob on a param and keeps the first. The order is the declared order of the params, skipping hidden ones; pass mountConsole(el, app, { learnOrder: ['hue', 'size'] }) for your own. The logic is LearnWizard in @openav/mapping: jsCopy

Software that should follow the show (a DAW launching a clip per segment, a lighting desk jumping scenes) cannot read the score, but it can read MIDI. ScoreMidi (@openav/midi) turns segment changes and cues into notes and CCs. It is off unless you ask: jsCopy optiondefaultmeaning channel15MIDI channel 1 to 16 segment{ note: 36 }note: base note, the note sent is note + index. cc: a CC whose value is the index. velocity. false turns segment markers off cue{ note: 84 }note for every cue, notes: { 'seg.name': note } for particular ones, cc whose value is the cue's number in the cut. false turns cue markers off length0.15seconds before a marker note's note-off scrubfalsealso mark when the playhead is moved by hand. By default markers go out only while the show plays (or a hold is released), so dragging the scrubber does not launch clips A reset never sends. Everything goes through the Midi engine's own noteOn/cc, so the MIDI OUT meter shows it and panic() silences it. In code: new ScoreMidi({ midi, channel, segment, cue }), then .segment({ index, cause }) and .cue({ name, n }).

A show that keeps two time lines (a story time that old logic reads and a show time the audience lives) needs a way to say which engine follows which: weather that never stops, a city that pauses while an inserted segment plays. That is a clock per engine. This framework has one time line, the show's T, so there is nothing for a clock to choose between, and a segment module that wants to pause an engine simply stops advancing it (ctx.t is its own clock, ctx.held another). If a real show brings back the two-time-line case, a clocks table belongs in the cut next to segments. Until then it would be machinery with no user.

open-audiovisual models MIDI controllers as data: one JSON file per device, with the faceplate layout, every control's exact MIDI message, LED feedback, how to recognise its port, and the document each number came from. The same file drives an on-screen controller you can play, follows the real device when you plug it in, and can be dropped into any web page. Every device is on the controllers page.

htmlCopy That is the whole integration. The element works without Web MIDI (Safari, iPad): it plays and fires events; only hardware and MIDI out report that they are unavailable. It never asks for MIDI permission unless you turn on hardware, midi-out or learn. Safari has none because WebKit has not implemented it (bug 107250, still open). AttributeWhat it does profilewhich device: an id, a short name, or a URL to your own profile JSON layoutauto, face (as it looks) or stack (re-gridded for a phone held upright) hardwareon, or ask for a button: the real device moves the on-screen one midi-outa port name (IAC, loopMIDI), /regex/, or ask: what you play is sent there channel1–16, when your unit is set to another channel picker, readout, learn, followdevice picker, last-message line, learn button, show whatever known device you plug in
jsCopy Other events: noteon, noteoff, connect, disconnect, status, profilechange, ready, error. All bubble and cross the shadow root. Every field of every payload is in packages/midi/README.md.
jsCopy Inside a show, do not read midi/lpd8/k1 in update(): route it to a param with controllerRoutes(profile, { k1: 'hue' }) (rule 1 in AGENTS.md). Example 09 does this for six devices at once.

For places that only take an iframe: htmlCopy The frame posts { source: 'openav', type, frame, detail } to its parent for every event, and accepts { target: 'openav', type: 'set' | 'ingest' | 'press' | 'release' | 'reset' | 'profile' | 'layout' | 'get', … }. Add origin=https://your.site to talk to your page only.

macOS: Audio MIDI Setup → Window → Show MIDI Studio → IAC Driver → “Device is online”. Windows 11: the built-in Windows MIDI Services (released 2026-02-17, rolled out in stages to 24H2 and 25H2) share MIDI ports between apps and include a loopback, and Microsoft's announcement says web pages using Web MIDI can use it (Windows blog). We have not tested it with open-audiovisual. Older Windows: install loopMIDI and add a port; that still works. <oav-controller profile="akai-lpd8" midi-out="IAC"> (on Windows, give the name of the port you made or the one Windows shows). In Ableton Live, turn on Track and Remote for that input; in TouchDesigner, a MIDI In CHOP on it; in Resolume, Preferences → MIDI. Hands on the screen are sent; your real hardware is not forwarded (the DAW already hears it). The engine never listens to IAC inputs, and the element mutes an input named like its output, so nothing loops.

So the project can see where its controllers and shows end up, the packages send one anonymous hit per page load to Google Analytics 4 (the openaudiovisual.com property, G-1YG2JHK2WT): eventwhenparams oav_embed_loadan <oav-controller>, createController() or the iframe startsoav_kind (element · headless · iframe), oav_profile, oav_host, oav_version oav_hardware_connecta real controller is plugged in and matchedoav_kind, oav_profile, oav_host, oav_version oav_show_startcreateShow() startsoav_kind (show), oav_host, oav_version oav_host is the origin of the page it runs on (for the iframe, the page that holds it), never the path, query or title. Nothing anyone plays is sent, no cookies are set, and the client id is random for every page load, so visitors can't be followed. No gtag.js is loaded: a page with its own Google Analytics keeps its dataLayer untouched. Nothing is sent from localhost, LAN addresses, file:// or openaudiovisual.com itself, or when the browser sends Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control. Turn it off: <oav-controller telemetry="off"> · createController(p, { telemetry: false }) · createShow({ telemetry: false }) · the iframe's ?telemetry=0 · or globalThis.OPENAV_TELEMETRY = false before anything loads. Source: packages/midi/telemetry.js.

Copy the closest file in packages/midi/profiles/, or a generic layout. Write each control's type and message from the manual's MIDI implementation chart. Cite every source; mark anything unconfirmed "verified": false with a note. validateProfile(profile) lists every problem; npm test checks every shipped profile. Try it with <oav-controller profile="./my-device.json">, then register it in profiles/index.js and open a pull request. No manual: choose a generic layout, press Learn, move your controls in order, and keep controller.exportMapping() as the start of a profile.

Any p5.js sketch (OpenProcessing, the p5 editor, your own page) can be played from a MIDI controller, from a controller drawn on screen, or from a phone, by adding one line at the top: jsCopy On OpenProcessing you can instead paste the URL into Sketch → Libraries → + (custom library). Both work in p5 1.x and 2.x global mode, and nothing has to be called in setup(). A sketch that carries this line, playable right now: example 15.

jsCopy readvalue knob1 … knob8, knob(n)0..1, numbered as printed on the controller fader1 … fader8, fader(n)0..1 pad1 … pad16, pad(n)the velocity while the pad is held, 0 when released note, velocitythe last key (MIDI number) and how hard (0..1) noteIsPressed, noteIsDown(60)like keyIsPressed and keyIsDown() definecalled when notePressed(note, velocity), noteReleased(note)a key goes down / up (a pad too, unless you define padPressed) knobMoved(n, value), faderMoved(n, value)a knob or fader moves padPressed(n, velocity), padReleased(n)a pad is hit / let go Knob 1 is knob 1 on whichever controller played it: the controller profiles say which MIDI message each knob sends (MiniLab 3's knob 1 is CC 74, LPD8's is CC 70). On a controller OAV has no profile for, the first knob you turn becomes knob1, the next knob2. A sketch that already has its own note, velocity or knob1 keeps it.

Wherever a note number goes, a note name goes too (0.8): jsCopy writeyou get noteNumber('C4')60; a number comes back as it is, held to 0..127 noteName(61)'C#4'; noteName(61, { flats: true }) is 'Db4', noteName(61, { octave: false }) is 'C#' noteFreq('A4'), noteFreq(69)440 (Hz), for a sketch that makes its own sound; noteFreq(69.5) is a quarter tone up noteIsDown('C4'), midi.isDown('C4'), midi.play('C#4', 0.8)the same as with 60, 61 A name is a letter A to G (either case), an optional # or b (♯ and ♭ too), and the octave number: C4, c#4, Db3, F♯2, C-1 (0) up to G9 (127). C4 is 60, the scientific pitch notation the course modules use; some software (Ableton, Yamaha) calls 60 "C3", so a name copied from there is one octave off. These are also the names Strudel writes (c4 e4 g4, # for sharp, b for flat). Anything else, such as H4 or C-2, stops with a one-line card saying how to write it. notePressed(note, velocity) still hands you the number: noteName(note) writes it back as a name.

OP Configurator 3000 (OPC, built into OpenProcessing) names a variable and its range. With this line on the page the controller is wired to those variables in order, with no mapping step: jsCopy Knobs drive the sliders in the order they are declared, the faders continue after the knobs, and pads drive toggles and buttons. OPC's panel moves with the knob, and parameterChanged() fires as usual. OpenProcessing's OPC panel can also learn hardware by itself (its MIDI switch); once that mapping is seen working, hardware is left to it and this line keeps wiring the on-screen controller and the phone, which OpenProcessing cannot see. Avoid OPC names that are also p5 functions (hue, fill): p5 1.x clashes with them. One knob, one job. If the sketch also reads knob1 itself, knob 1 is the sketch's: the first OPC slider no longer follows it (drag it on OPC's panel), the other knobs stay wired, and a hint says so once. The first line of the 🎹 panel is the wiring, for example knob1 → knob1 (sketch; radius by its slider) · knob2 → speed (OPC).

The same line reads the microphone, and the sketch reads it the same way: as variables. jsCopy readvalue micLevel0..1, how loud it sounds: the room's own noise is 0, talking is about 0.4–0.6, shouting is near 1 bass, mid, treble0..1, the energy in 20–250 Hz, 250–2000 Hz and 2000–8000 Hz beattrue for one frame per beat, like mouseIsPressed while a button is down micIsOnwhether the microphone is running startMic(), stopMic()turn it on or off from code (they return a promise) micSensitivity(2)twice as sensitive; micSensitivity() returns the current value write this functionwhen it is called beatDetected(level)a beat: a jump in loudness over what the room has been doing (level 0..1) kickDetected(level), snareDetected(level), hatDetected(level)a hit in the low, middle or high band (20–120 Hz, 150–800 Hz, 6–14 kHz) It is off until the sketch asks. Nothing is requested when the page loads. The first time the sketch reads micLevel, bass, mid, treble or beat, or calls startMic(), the browser asks for the microphone; until the answer arrives every value is 0. A sketch that defines beatDetected() and reads nothing starts it on the first click or key. In the 🎹 panel the 🎤 button turns it on and off by hand and shows the level, and it says so when the browser blocked the microphone (click it again after allowing it from the address bar). Click first, if the browser wants one. Browsers keep audio quiet until the page has been clicked. This file asks as soon as draw() reads a value and starts the microphone again on the first click or key if the browser held it back, so no userStartAudio() is needed. Next to p5.sound. The analysis is @openav/audio (an AnalyserNode), loaded from next to this file the first time it is needed, with its own AudioContext. p5.sound (p5.AudioIn, p5.FFT) can run on the same page; the two microphones do not share anything, and none of these names is a p5 or p5.sound name. It works in p5 1.x and 2.x global mode. How loud is loud. micLevel is a loudness in decibels, measured from the room: its bottom follows the room's own noise (it settles in a second or two, and rises at most 1.5 dB a second, so a voice never becomes the new silence), and −10 dBFS, shouting into a laptop, is 1. So 50 + micLevel * 300 visibly grows when someone talks. A quiet or far microphone: micSensitivity(3) (+9.5 dB on micLevel, ×3 on the bands, still capped at 1). The raw numbers are OAVp5.mic.rms (0..1), OAVp5.mic.db and OAVp5.mic.floor (the room, in dBFS). OAVp5.mic.on('beat', fn) is the same as defining beatDetected, and returns a function that stops it. records.n: Sound: what is played is heard
records.x: jsCopy call / readvalue startSound(instrument)turn sound on (default 'piano'), or switch instruments while it plays stopSound()turn it off soundIsOnwhether notes are heard now The instruments are those of @openav/sound: piano (the Salamander grand; its 2 MB of samples load the first time, and the electric piano plays meanwhile, or instead if they cannot load), epiano, organ, strings, choir, harp, marimba, vibraphone, xylophone, glockenspiel, music-box and the synth/… presets. In the 🎹 panel, 🔊 turns sound on and off and shows a picker with every instrument and the loading progress. Off until asked. Nothing loads before startSound() or 🔊; then @openav/sound from next to this file and Tone.js 15 from jsDelivr (the option tone=<url> loads it from elsewhere). The first click. Browsers play audio only after the page has been clicked, and a key on a MIDI keyboard does not count. A sketch that calls startSound() in setup() is heard from the first click or key; until then the 🔊 on the 🎹 button is yellow. Pads are drums. Notes on MIDI channel 10 (MiniLab 3 and LPD8 pads, the General MIDI drum channel) play the drum kit, not the piano. The sustain pedal holds notes. No code at all. ?oav_sound=piano on the page (any instrument id; on OpenProcessing ?sketch_oav_sound=piano) makes any sketch heard from the first click; sound=off keeps it silent. A sketch that plays and draws, ready to open: p5/examples/keys/.

jsCopy readvalue drumsAreOnwhether the machine is playing drumStep0..15, the step that just played drumBar1, 2, 3 …, counted from startDrums() drumBpmthe tempo (the grid's slider changes it too) drumPhase0..1, how far through the bar, smoothly, as heard: rotate(drumPhase * TWO_PI) turns once a bar beatPhase0..1, how far through the beat (a quarter note): 1 - beatPhase swells on each beat and shrinks to the next startDrums(pattern, bpm), stopDrums()start (or change the pattern and tempo while it plays), stop write this functionwhen it is called drumHit(lane, velocity)every hit, every drum (a line of rhythm's crash, ride or toms too) kickDetected(level), snareDetected(level), hatDetected(level)a kick; a snare, a clap or a rim; a hat (closed, open or pedal) beatDetected(level)a kick or a snare, once per step (and beat is true for a frame) rhythmChanged(src, how)the line changed: startDrums(), a click on a cell, a line typed, ↶ (0.7) A microphone sketch moves over unchanged. Each hit calls the same functions the microphone does, so a sketch written for the microphone reacts to the machine as it is. Once a sketch has started the machine, defining kickDetected() no longer opens the microphone on the first click (a sketch that reads micLevel still asks, and then both call it). Patterns. 'four on floor', breakbeat, 'half time', latin, sparse, your own startDrums({ kick: 'x...x...x...x...', snare: '....x.......x...', hat: 'x.x.x.x.x.x.x.x.' }) (a lane left out is silent), or one line of rhythm (below). The card. The lanes are named in the page's language (大鼓 小鼓 鈸 拍手 in a Chinese browser), the bar it is in shows beside the tempo, and the step that sounds is a yellow column (13:1 against the dark card, readable on a projector). Where the grid sits. At the top centre: on OpenProcessing between the 🎹 and OPC's icon and clear of the console, and below the 🎹 panel while that is open. – folds it, × stops the machine, and 🥁 in the 🎹 panel starts and stops it with no code at all. The kit. @openav/drums' synthesized kit (no samples), heard from the first click like sound; the callbacks run from the start either way. On time, however heavy the sketch. The hits are handed to the kit ahead of time, on its audio clock: a heartbeat in a Web Worker wakes every 25 ms and schedules what falls in the next 0.1 s at its exact time. Measured on the kit's own output with a draw() that keeps the page busy 30 ms a frame, the kick-to-kick interval varies by 0.000 ms (0.5, which played each hit in the frame it was due, varied by 15 ms). The callbacks still come in a frame: the one in…

jsCopy Any text that is not a pattern name is a line of rhythm; names, grids and numbers work exactly as before. The line shows over the grid, and the word that sounds lights up and fades. writemeanse.g. a worda drum: bd kick, sd snare, hh hat, oh open hat, cp clap, rim, lt mt ht toms, cr crash, rd ride, cb cowbell"bd sd bd sd" ~a rest"bd ~ sd ~" spacethe words share the bar evenly"bd hh sd hh" [ ]a group shares one place"bd [sd sd]" *nn times in that place"hh*8" ,another line on top"bd*4, hh*8" < >one per bar, in turn"<bd*4 [bd ~ bd ~]>" (k,n)k hits spread over n steps"bd(3,8)" The whole list is in @openav/pattern, loaded from next to oav-p5.js with the drums. Drums the grid has no lane for (crash, ride, toms, open hat) get a row of their own; a hit off the sixteen steps (a triplet) is drawn where it falls inside its step. A mistake in startDrums("…") shows a card in the page's language with the character it is at, why, and how to fix it, and the machine plays 'four on floor' meanwhile; 'x...x...' on its own (one lane of the grid) says to put it inside { kick: … }. A line copied from strudel.cc works too: startDrums('s("bd*4, [~ sd]*2").fast(2)') plays [bd*4, [~ sd]*2]*2. s("…"), sound("…"), with ", ' or ` quotes, several of them ($: s(…)) as layers, .fast(n) and .slow(n); setcpm(110/4) or setcps(…) sets the tempo when startDrums() is given none. .bank("…") is left out (OAV plays its own synthesized kit) and anything else in the chain (.jux(rev), .every(…), .gain(…)) gets a card that says OAV does not do it yet and points at Open in Strudel; the rest plays. The way of writing one line of rhythm comes from TidalCycles / Strudel (strudel.cc); OAV implements it independently from their public documentation.

records.n: The cells and the line edit each other
records.x: Since 0.7 the line over the grid is always there (a preset shows the line its grid is: 'four on floor' is bd*4, [~ sd]*2, hh*8) and both ways work: Click a cell: the line is rewritten the way a person would write it, and the machine plays the new line at once. Steady hits become bd*4 / hh*8, one hit per group [~ sd]*2, a Euclidean rhythm bd(3,8) (with its rotation: bd(3,8,2) starts two steps later), anything else beat by beat: bd [~ ~ ~ bd] bd*2 ~. Lines are joined with , . When the line holds more than sixteen steps can (triplets, < >, /2, ?, bd:2), the first click shows a card saying what would go, and the next click rewrites it. Type in the line: click it, change it; Enter, or a pause of 400 ms, plays it and the cells follow. A mistake marks the word in red, a card says what is wrong, and the last line that worked keeps playing (not 'four on floor'). Escape drops what is not played yet. Typed keys never reach the sketch's keyPressed(). ↶ on the card (or ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z after touching the card) goes back one line; OAVp5.drums.history lists them. Copy puts startDrums("…", 110) on the clipboard, ready to paste into setup(). Open in Strudel opens the same line at strudel.cc in a new tab, as s("…") with setcpm(bpm/4) (one OAV bar is one Strudel cycle of four beats; strudel.cc's docs: setcpm(bpm/bpc)). OAVp5.drums.strudelUrl is the link. jsCopy OAVp5.drums.src is the line that plays, OAVp5.drums.edit("…") plays a line as if typed, OAVp5.drums.undo() goes back. Keys that swap the rhythm, step back and open Strudel: p5/examples/rhythm-lab/.

The card is part of the page, not the canvas, so a recording never shows it. drawRhythm() draws the rhythm on the canvas: jsCopy drawRhythm(x, y, w, h, style, options): style is 'grid', 'circle' or 'spiral'; a hit lights up the moment it is heard (the clock drumPhase reads) and a triplet sits where it falls. Options: colors ({ kick: '#f66', … }, any p5 color), color (one for all), off (the empty steps), playhead (a color, or false), bg, bars (spiral). Drawn inside push() / pop() with p5's own shapes, in 2D and WEBGL, p5 1.x and 2.x; in WEBGL (0, 0) is the middle of the canvas: drawRhythm(-width / 2, -height / 2, width, height, 'circle'). With no box it draws a strip along the bottom ('grid') or a square in the middle. A sketch with all three: p5/examples/rhythm-visual/.

The drum machine is also the clock: sixteen steps a bar, counted from startDrums(). Declare what happens at which bar: jsCopy call / read / define cue(bar, name, every)at bar bar (1 is the first, 4.5 is halfway through bar 4); every bars again if given cueNamethe last cue that fired ('' before the first) cueFired(name, bar)a cue's bar has come barStarted(bar), stepStarted(step, bar)the first step of every bar; every step The same cue() twice adds nothing, so it may also sit in draw(). On one step the cues fire in the order they were declared, then barStarted, stepStarted and that step's hits. A silent clock: startDrums({}). The whole of it, ready to open: p5/examples/drums/; a line of rhythm with drumPhase and beatPhase: p5/examples/rhythm/; the rhythm drawn on the canvas: p5/examples/rhythm-visual/.

records.n: Values over time: lag, env, speed, spring, trail
records.x: A knob or micLevel jumps; what looks good is how it moves between the jumps. TouchDesigner does this with CHOPs; the same operators are here, one call each in draw(), nothing to declare, and seconds are seconds (the same curve at 30 and at 144 fps): jsCopy TouchDesigneroav-p5 Lag CHOP (Lag 1 / Lag 2)lag(value, up, down)follows value: up seconds while it rises, down while it falls (down = up if left out; 0.1) Trigger CHOP (attack, decay)env('kick', attack, decay), trigger('boom')0..1: up to 1 in attack seconds after each event, back to 0 in decay (0.01, 0.3). Events: 'kick' 'snare' 'hat' 'beat' (the microphone or the drum machine, the hits kickDetected hears), 'note' (any key), 'bar' 'step' (the drums), a cue's name, trigger('boom'); or a switch: env(mouseIsPressed, …) Speed CHOPspeed(rate)adds rate every second: rotate(speed(TWO_PI)) turns once a second Spring CHOPspring(value, stiffness, damping)follows like a mass on a spring (100, 6: two or three bounces; damping 20: none) Trail CHOPtrail(value, seconds)the last seconds (2) as an array, 60 values a second, oldest first, the newest last Slope CHOPslope(value)how fast it changes, per second Count CHOPcount(beat), count(beat, 4), count('kick')how many times it turned on; with 4: 0 1 2 3 0 …; a name: how many of those events so far a CHOP's viewerscope(value, 'label')a small plot in the corner of the page (below) drawTrail(values, x, y, w, h)the same plot on the canvas, in the work and in a recording Seconds, the same as in TouchDesigner. A lag's seconds mean what a Lag CHOP's do: about the time the value takes to follow 90% of a jump, so lag(x, 0.1) here moves like a Lag CHOP set to 0.1 (Lag CHOP). Underneath it is a one-pole lag with a time constant of seconds ÷ 2.3 (ln 10); @openav/mapping's smooth keeps its own 63% time constant. Attack and decay are lengths in both. Nothing to declare. The first lag() in draw() keeps the first lag's memory, the second the second, every frame; spring(), speed(), trail() … are counted each on their own. Put one inside an if, or in a loop whose length changes, and the order slips: a card says so, and from then on oav-p5 matches each call by the line it is written on. The sure way is a name, a string at the end: lag(p.size, 0.1, 0.5, 'p' + p.id). A named one is the same wherever it is called, draw(), setup() or mousePressed(); an unnamed one outside draw() has nothing to remember by and returns its input (speed 0, trail []), and a card says that too. env(), trigger() and count('kick') are about events and work anywhere. A sketch with its own speed or count keeps it;…

records.n: Recording: a video with its sound
records.x: jsCopy call / read / define startRecording(), startRecording(seconds), startRecording({ seconds, fps, mic, name, canvas, bitrate })record the canvas and the sketch's sound; with seconds it stops by itself; a take is 5 minutes at most. canvas is the canvas to record (a p5 canvas or createGraphics(); the default is the biggest p5 canvas on the page), bitrate is bits a second (the default follows the canvas size and frame rate, 4 to 80 Mb/s) stopRecording()stop; the file downloads recordingIsOnwhether a take is running recordingSaved(info)the file is saved: name, seconds, bytes, format, width, height, audio, sources, warnings, blob, url In the 🎹 panel, ⏺ starts and stops a take with no code; while it runs, the 🎹 button shows a red dot and the time (a click on the dot stops it). 📷 saves the canvas as a PNG. What is in the video. The p5 canvas at its own pixel size (a retina screen doubles it), 30 frames a second, and every sound this file makes: startSound(), the drum machine and the pads, the microphone while it is on, and p5.sound 1.x, mixed into one track while the speakers play as before. The 🎹, the drum grid, the cards and OPC's panel are not on the canvas, so they are not in the video. The file. MP4 (H.264 + AAC), which Instagram, YouTube and every editor take, wherever the browser can write it: Chrome 126 and later, Edge, Safari. Elsewhere (Firefox, an older Chrome) WebM, and a card says Instagram will not take it. It is named oav-20261015-183005.mp4; on a computer it lands in Downloads, on a phone a Share button on the card saves it to the photo library or sends it to Instagram. Checked after every take. A card says what was recorded (format, length, size, with or without sound) and, when something is wrong, what and why: nothing reached the recording although a sound was on (no click on the page yet, nothing played), WebM, an almost empty file, a black video of a canvas that was not black (Safari recording a WebGL canvas, WebKit 229611), an image from another site on the canvas (no CORS), no recorder in this browser. The microphone is in the take while it is on: wear headphones, or the speakers are recorded twice. record=nomic leaves it out. p5.sound. p5.sound 1.x (the one for p5 1.x) is recorded. The p5.sound made for p5 2.x connects each sound straight to the speakers, with no output a recording can tap: it is not in the take, and a card says so. Switch the sketch to p5 1.11, or use startSound() and startDrums(). Sound the sketch makes with its own Tone.js or Web Audio code is not recorded either. Stills. 📷 (or OAVp5.record.shot()) saves…

inputhow a real controllerWeb MIDI in Chrome, Edge and Firefox; the browser asks once the on-screen controller🎹 opens <oav-controller>, which follows the controller you plug in a phone📱 in that panel shows a QR code; the phone's remote page MIDI tab plays the sketch All three arrive as the same MIDI bytes, so the sketch cannot tell them apart (midi.last.source can). Safari and iPad have no Web MIDI; the on-screen controller and the phone still work there. A sketch that uses Web MIDI itself (navigator.requestMIDIAccess, WebMidi.js) also hears the screen and the phone, as one more input called OAV Virtual MIDI. Other programs are a fourth input (0.7). What a program plays into OAV Virtual MIDI's output — Strudel's .midi('OAV Virtual MIDI') — reaches the sketch at the moment it was stamped with (midi.last.source is virtual-out); an external MIDI clock moves drumPhase, drumBar and a drum machine; and link=<room> brings another tab's or another computer's programs into this sketch. All of it: With Strudel.

Nobody watches OpenProcessing's console while playing, so problems are said on the page: a small card beside the 🎹, never over the middle of the canvas, in the browser's language, once per page, with a × to close it. Each card says what happened, why, and what to press, and the console gets the same sentence. The microphone: refused (the lock left of the address → allow → click the canvas), refused by the computer's settings, by an embed without allow="microphone", missing, held by another app (Zoom, OBS), an http: page, or the browser still asking. MIDI: no Web MIDI (Safari, iPad: use the 🎹 or a phone), or the permission refused. Only for a sketch that plays from MIDI; a sketch that uses none of this never sees a card. Your own code: an error inside notePressed(), kickDetected(), drumHit() and the other callbacks shows the message with the file and line, and the sketch keeps running. A sketch that declares its own note or knob1 (let, var, function) keeps it, and the card says what to read instead (midi.last.note, knob(1)). Sound and drums: waiting for the first click, the piano still loading (the electric piano meanwhile), an instrument that failed (the fallback plays), Tone.js unreachable, the drum machine playing silently until a click. Recording: started (what it hears, how to stop), saved (format, length, size, sound), a take with no sound in it, WebM (not for Instagram), a black take, an almost empty file, a canvas with another site's image, no recorder in this browser. ?oav_hints=off (or window.OAV_P5 = { hints: 'off' }) keeps them in the console only; OAVp5.hints lists what was said. 🩺 Check-up. 🩺 in the 🎹 panel (or OAVp5.check()) shows the version, the page, the browser, the microphone, MIDI, sound, drums, recording (MP4 or WebM here, the last take), the wiring, the sketch's own names and the hints so far, as one card to screenshot, with a copy button and a link to the full device check.

Hydra has a loader of its own; the same file works there, and Hydra's arrow functions read the variables each frame: jsCopy jsCopy note, velocity, knob1 … knob8, fader1 …, pad1 …, drumStep and the 🎹 on-screen controller are there the same way. Hydra is not p5, so there are no notePressed() callbacks to define; subscribe instead: midi.on('notePressed', (note, velocity) => { … }) or OAVp5.drums.on('hit', (lane, velocity) => { … }) (each returns a function that unsubscribes). Checked against hydra-synth 1.4.0, the library the editor runs (p5/test/hydra-smoke.cjs).

Why prepend. p5's friendly-error checker reads the last <script> on the page as your sketch. Put first, this file is never mistaken for your code. Why one asynchronous line is enough. p5 starts global mode on the window's load event, and a script inserted while the page is loading holds load back until it has run, so knob1 already exists in setup(). When the line does not load (offline, a typo in the URL), code that reads knob1 stops with knob1 is not defined. Embedding a sketch elsewhere. OpenProcessing's own pages allow MIDI and the microphone in the sketch frame. The embed code it gives you does not: add allow="midi" to that <iframe> if the embedded sketch should hear a hardware controller, and allow="microphone" if it should hear the microphone. Options, MIDI-level access and tests: p5/README.md. Examples: p5/examples/particles/, p5/examples/opc/, p5/examples/mic/, p5/examples/keys/, p5/examples/drums/, p5/examples/rhythm/, p5/examples/rhythm-visual/, p5/examples/rhythm-lab/, p5/examples/record/, p5/examples/lag/, p5/examples/chop/, p5/examples/with-strudel/ and p5/examples/note-names/.

Strudel is a live-coding environment for music in the browser, a JavaScript version of TidalCycles. OAV is a separate program. The two run side by side the way two programs on a stage do: Strudel plays, and OAV brings what Strudel does not have — knobs on screen and on a phone, a microphone that is analysed, Web MIDI where the browser has none — and draws what Strudel plays in a p5.js sketch, on the same page or in another tab or on another computer. They meet through MIDI (OAV's virtual port, "OAV Virtual MIDI") and through the page's own variables (knob1, micLevel, drumPhase). OAV never loads or calls any of Strudel's code. Everything on this page was run on strudel.cc as a user runs it (its editor, Ctrl+Enter, its documented functions): p5/test/strudel-smoke.cjs does it again.

Strudel → settings → prebake, add one line at the end, save: jsCopy Single quotes. Strudel reads text in double quotes (and backticks) as mini-notation: a URL in double quotes is a [mini] parse error. Why the prebake. It runs before your code, also after a reload (about 2.5 s after the editor appears), so OAV is on the page before anything opens MIDI. If Strudel's midin() ran before OAV loaded, midin('OAV Virtual MIDI') gets nothing and says nothing: reload. 🩺 then shows "no program has asked OAV Virtual MIDI for MIDI". The line can also be the first line of your code. Options go on the line before it: window.OAV_P5 = { link: 'my-room' }. Strudel's share button puts the prebake into the link (with "share with patterns" ticked): whoever opens it gets OAV too. On strudel.cc OAV changes its manners. It does not ask for MIDI when it loads (hardware=click: Strudel's midin() asks). The 🎹 panel is a box in the corner, a third of the window high, so the code stays in view. One card says which names Strudel already has — note, velocity, beat are Strudel's functions, OAV leaves them alone — and what to read instead: OAVp5.last.note, OAVp5.last.value, OAVp5.mic.on('beat', fn). knob1, micLevel, drumPhase and the rest are free names there.

records.n: Recipe 1: knobs, a phone and the microphone as Strudel's parameters
records.x: Strudel's signal() turns a function into a parameter; OAV's names are plain values a function can return. jsCopy knob1 moves with knob 1 of the 🎹 on screen, of a MIDI controller, or of a phone (🎹 → 📱, scan the code). knob(2), fader1, pad1 are there too. Measured: knob 1 at 0, the kick is silent; at 127, it is heard (RMS 0.58). Strudel reads the value when it schedules, 0.2–0.3 s before the sound: a knob is heard that much later. micLevel, bass, mid, treble are OAV's analysis of the microphone (Strudel has none); reading one asks for the microphone. Wear headphones: the microphone hears the speakers, and gain(signal(() => micLevel)) feeds back. Strudel's own MIDI input works on OAV's port too, also in Safari (no Web MIDI there; OAV's port is virtual): jsCopy Knob 1 of the on-screen MiniLab 3 is CC 74. midikeys('OAV Virtual MIDI') makes the 🎹 keys and the phone Strudel's keyboard.

records.n: Recipe 2: Strudel plays, a p5 sketch draws
records.x: On the same page. Send to OAV's port: jsCopy Strudel hands each note over 0.21–0.32 s early with the moment it should sound; OAV waits for that moment and then calls notePressed(note, velocity) (in Strudel, with no sketch: OAVp5.on('notePressed', fn)), moves knob1 for a CC, plays a pad. Measured on strudel.cc: each note is heard within 5 ms of its timestamp (10 notes, at most 4.5 ms late; p5/test/strudel-smoke.cjs), and drumPhase follows Strudel's clock to 0.1 ms. What arrives on the port is never handed back to OAV's input, so midikeys('OAV Virtual MIDI') played into .midi('OAV Virtual MIDI') is one echo, not a loop. Strudel's clock. MIDI counts 24 clocks a beat, so a cycle of one 4-beat bar sends 96: jsCopy drumPhase, beatPhase, drumBar, drumStep and drumBpm follow it. A drum machine started with startDrums() plays at Strudel's tempo, on Strudel's downbeat, and starts and stops with it (the card says "following an external clock · 128 BPM"). Measured at 128 bpm: drumPhase within 1.2 ms of Strudel's bar (median 0.04 ms), every kick within 6 ms of Strudel's beat (three runs); Strudel's start, which arrives three times with one timestamp, counts once. Without a clock nothing changes; clock=off ignores one. In another tab, or on another computer. Give both pages the same room. In Strudel's prebake: jsCopy and in the p5 sketch (OpenProcessing: before the one line; or ?sketch_oav_link=my-room on the page's address): jsCopy Everything Strudel sends to OAV's port — notes, CCs, the clock — reaches every other OAV page in the room, through the same relay the phones use. 🎹 grows a 🔗: green when another page is there; the panel says the room, the pages and the trip. The receiving page plays each note when Strudel plays it, not when it arrives: it lines the two clocks up from the fastest trips it has seen and the round trips both pages measure (packages/relay/link.js explains how), and Strudel's quarter-second head start covers the trip. Measured with two tabs on one Mac over wss://remote.cheyuwu.com (one way ≈ 61 ms): notes within −3 … +7 ms of Strudel's timestamps (two runs). Across two computers add the difference between the two halves of a round trip (usually a few ms). Keep the default relay (wss://): Chrome does not let strudel.cc reach a relay on your own machine or network (ws://127.0.0.1… is blocked by its local-network checks). On a network whose jitter is longer than Strudel's head start, linkdelay= (ms) buffers more. A page never sends on what it received, and a program that plays a linked note back out is caught as an echo. The room is the phones'…

records.n: Recipe 3: Strudel, Hydra and OAV on one page
records.x: With OAV in the prebake: jsCopy Hydra turns once a bar on Strudel's clock (through drumPhase), knob 1 drives Hydra and Strudel at once, and the microphone colours the picture.

Set before the line (window.OAV_P5 = { … }), or ?oav_key=value on a p5 page's address. keyvaluesdefault linka room name (letters, digits, -, _): pages in it hear each other's programsnone linkdelaymilliseconds of extra buffer on a linked page's notes0 clockfollow (an external MIDI clock moves drumPhase and the drums) · offfollow strudelauto (strudel.cc, or Strudel's functions already on the page) · on · offauto compacton (the panel as a box in the corner) · offon in Strudel hardwareauto · click · offclick in Strudel

Strudel is © its contributors (begun by Felix Roos and Alex McLean), free software under the GNU Affero General Public License v3: strudel.cc, source at codeberg.org/uzu/strudel. TidalCycles, whose way of writing patterns Strudel carries to the browser, is Alex McLean's. Music you make with Strudel is yours (Strudel's FAQ). OAV is MIT-licensed and a separate program. It contains no Strudel code, does not load @strudel/* at run time and calls none of Strudel's functions: it only looks at the page's address and at which names the page already has, to choose its manners. The two meet the way two programs on a stage meet, over MIDI. OAV's own rhythm strings (startDrums("bd*4, hh*8"), @openav/pattern) are an independent implementation of the TidalCycles / Strudel way of writing rhythm, from their public documentation. Please do not ask Strudel's community for help with OAV: OAV's issues are on GitHub.

Phones and iPads can be controllers: their motion sensors, a piano, and a TouchOSC-style control panel that grows from the world's params. Three packages do it, each usable alone: packagerole @openav/relaya zero-dependency WebSocket relay with rooms, and its browser client @openav/surfacethe control-surface widgets, the layout JSON, autoSurface(params) @openav/remotethe phone app (tabs 感測 sensors · 琴鍵 keys · 控制台 control · MIDI) and the show-side adapter To the mapper, a phone is one more input: it publishes signals, and routes connect them to params.

Run node serve.js on the show machine. It serves the pages and hosts the relay at /relay; nothing else is needed. Open a show that declares modules: { remote: true }, for example http://localhost:8080/examples/08-remote-surface/. The join card at the top left of the stage shows the URL a phone should open, with the show machine's LAN address filled in (the page asks serve.js for it at /__info) and the room: http://<lan-ip>:8080/packages/remote/?room=default. Open that URL on a phone on the same network. The card counts connected phones. The card also draws a QR code of that URL: point a phone's camera at it.

There is no serve.js there, so no relay of its own. A show that declares modules: { remote: true } uses the public relay (wss://remote.cheyuwu.com/relay) instead, and the card says so (public relay). Open example 08 on the computer, scan the QR code with the phone, and the phone's faders move the show. The room is random (show- plus 10 characters), made once and kept in this browser's localStorage, so a reload keeps the same room and two visitors never share one. A room name declared in the show (room: 'main') is ignored here for that reason; ?room=class-7 in the page URL always wins, which is how a classroom puts everyone in one show. ?relay=wss://your.host/relay uses a relay of your own (the phone link carries it along); ?relay=off turns the remote off for that page. The choice is pickRelay() in @openav/remote/relay-pick: this machine or its LAN (localhost, 192.168.x.x, *.local…) keeps the same-origin /relay and works exactly as before; any other host gets the public relay. The public relay has no accounts and no authentication. The room name is the only secret, so treat the QR code like one: whoever scans it can drive that show. Don't put it on a slide you share.

/packages/remote/ is a single page with a status header (connection, latency, room, the phone's id) and tabs: 感測 (sensors): a tilt ball, acceleration and rotation readouts, a multi-touch pad, knocks (a sharp jolt of the phone), and light from the front camera. iOS needs a tap on 開始 (start) before it gives motion data. 琴鍵 (keys): a piano that is one row of about three octaves in landscape, and two stacked rows in portrait (the upper row continues the range). Vertical position on a key sets velocity; hold-to-sustain and octave buttons included. 控制台 (control): a control surface. Its layout comes from, in order: the ?surface=<layout.json url> query, the ?meta=<json url> query (its params go through autoSurface), whatever the show publishes over the relay, and finally a small generic panel so the page is never blank. MIDI: a virtual MIDI controller, the same one the show displays (MIDI controllers & embedding). querymeaning room=<name>the room to join (1–32 characters of A–Z a–z 0–9 _ -; anything else means default) tab=sense|keys|control|midithe tab to open first surface=<url>a layout JSON for the control tab meta=<url>a JSON file with a params array; the control tab becomes autoSurface(params) relay=ws://…a relay somewhere else than the page's own server (the QR code on the join card carries it when the show uses the public relay) Each phone keeps a short random id in localStorage; it is the <id> in phone/<id>/….

iOS Safari only gives motion sensors and the camera to pages served over https://. Touch, keys and the control surface work over plain http:// on the LAN. For tilt and knocks on an iPhone, reach serve.js through an HTTPS tunnel and open the tunnel's address on the phone; the relay follows the page's origin (wss:// on HTTPS pages). Android Chrome behaves the same for the camera.

modules: { remote: true } in createShow() (or mountRemoteHost() from @openav/remote/host) does five things, so the world stays ignorant of phones: joins the relay as the room's runner (the show); files every phone signal into signals, and mirrors phone/<id>/… to phone/any/…, which always holds the value from whichever phone sent it last; builds the control surface: world.surface if the world ships a layout, otherwise autoSurface(world.params); and publishes it to every phone, including phones that join later; adds the surface/… → param routes to the mapper (skipping pairs that are already there); sends param values back to the phones about 10 times a second, so faders follow the timeline and other controllers. modules.remote optiondefaultmeaning room?room= in the page URL, else 'default'the room name auto{}options for autoSurface (pairs, meters, style, perPage, smooth, title) surfaceworld.surfacean explicit layout (wins over the world's) feedbackHz10how often param values are echoed relaychosen by pickRelay()'wss://host/relay' for a relay of your own, false for no remote. Without it: same-origin /relay on this machine or LAN, the public relay on a static host. ?relay= in the page URL overrides it urlthe samealias of relay (and the option mountRemoteHost() takes: it appends role, room and id) Routes for sensors are written at author time with the phone/any/… alias, because nobody knows a stranger's device id in advance (example 08): jsCopy show.remote is the host: { relay, layout, routes, bindings, room, publish(), frame(dt, state), connect(), dispose() }.

A surface turns fingers into named, normalized signals. Every widget publishes under surface/<page>/<id>; when the widget's range is not 0..1, the unscaled value also goes out as …/raw. typepublishesnotes fader<id>orient: v, h or auto (follows the cell's shape) · double-tap resets to def knob<id>grab the rim to turn, the middle to drag encoder<id> (phase, wraps) and <id>/delta (turns)endless button<id> 1 / 0momentary; a pulse param fires on the rising edge toggle<id> 1 / 0 xy<id>/x, <id>/y, <id>/downspring: true returns to the centre bank<id>/1 … <id>/Ncount, labels; one finger paints across channels radio<id> = index / (n − 1), raw = indexoptions: [...] pads<id>/hit pulse { pad, row, col, vel }, <id>/<n> velocity while heldrows, cols (default 4 × 4), labels; n counts from 0; velocity = where you hit (top soft, bottom hard) keyboardmidi/note/on, midi/note/off, midi/cc/64the same names a hardware keyboard uses number<id>− / + buttons (hold repeats) and a field text<id>, a string pulseEnter or ↵ sends label, meternothingdisplay only; fed by surface.feedback(name, value) Common fields: id, type, label, min, max, def, step, unit, color (cyan amber magenta lime violet coral white), and target (a param key, or an array for xy and bank) for hand-written layouts. The phone keyboard's notes are { note, vel, velocity, ch: 1, device: 'surface' }.

A layout is data, like a route: shareable as a file, writable by an agent, publishable by a world. jsonCopy Phones get turned, so a page decides its arrangement like this: if the page has a portrait or landscape variant for the current orientation, use its grid (widgets missing from its place keep their base spot or fill free cells); otherwise, if the base grid already has the right shape, use it; otherwise auto-reflow: the same widgets, repacked row by row into half (portrait) or double (landscape) the columns. Rows are a count, not pixels, so the grid always fills the screen and nothing ever scrolls. Widgets without x/y are packed into free cells with a default size per type. validateLayout(layout) returns a list of problems (empty = fine); new Surface() throws with that list on a bad layout.

autoSurface(params, options) turns a world's params into a layout, the routes that drive the params, and the bindings for feedback: jsCopy How each param becomes a widget: paramwidget pulse: truebutton step: 1 and a range of 1 (two values)toggle step: 1 and three to seven valuesradio (labels from options, else the numbers) a pair listed in pairsone xy pad driving both anything elsea fader when there are six continuous params or fewer, knobs when there are more surface: { type, color, label } on the paramwhatever it says Options: pairs, meters (params to also show read-only), style ('auto', 'fader', 'knob'), perPage (default 8; a page that scrolls is a page that fails), smooth (default 0.04 s on continuous routes, to hide 30 Hz network steps), title. Each param group gets its own page.

Give a widget a target and routesFromLayout(layout, params) writes its route (the same shape autoSurface produces): xy maps x to the first target and y to the second, bank maps channel i to the i-th target. A world can carry its layout as world.surface; the show side then uses it instead of generating one.

Every control reads CSS custom properties on :root (THEME_VARS: --oav-bg, --oav-surface, --oav-accent, --oav-radius, --oav-touch-min (44 px) …). Override them to re-skin the whole surface. The rules: dark, ≥ 44 px touch targets, the live number always visible, pressed = border and glow in the widget's color, navigator.vibrate where it exists. @openav/surface also exports phone helpers: lockViewport() (no scrolling or zooming), keepAwake() (Wake Lock), toggleFullscreen(), canFullscreen(), haptic(ms).

Clients connect to ws://<host>/relay?role=controller|runner|monitor&room=<name>&id=<device>. A room is a name; peers in different rooms never hear each other. fromtowhat controller (a phone)runner + monitorsignal and batch runner (the show)monitorsignal and batch runnercontrollers + monitorsfeedback (meters, fader echo), config (the surface layout; replayed to phones that join later) monitornobody Messages are JSON: {"type":"signal","name":"phone/ab12/tilt/x","value":0.3,"t":…,"pulse"?:true}, {"type":"batch","items":[…]}, ping/pong, status (peer counts), feedback, config. Clients ignore types they do not know. When the runner leaves, the room forgets its config. Messages over 256 KB are ignored, frames over 1 MB close the connection, and a phone that stops answering pings (screen locked, Wi-Fi gone) is dropped within about 40 s. jsCopy Continuous values are re-sent once a second so a phone that joins late, or a show page reloaded mid-performance, is never stuck on stale defaults. Pulses are never batched or repeated: a note-on delivered twice is a bug. The client reconnects by itself (0.5 s, doubling up to 5 s). fileSignal(signals, name, value, { pulse }) is the receiving half of the wire format: it declares a name the first time it is heard (signalMeta() knows the ranges of phone/…, surface/… and midi/… names), fills in whichever velocity spelling a note message lacks (vel 0..1 or velocity 1..127), then pulses or sets. To run the relay without serve.js: node packages/relay/server.js [port] (default 7458, health at /health), or attach it to your own Node server with attachRelay(server, { path: '/relay' }) from @openav/relay/server.

records.n: The show page on a phone
records.x: When the show itself runs on a phone, it can read the phone's own motion sensors without a relay. localSensors(signals) publishes the same names under phone/local/…, mirrored to phone/any/…, so routes written for "the latest phone" work either way. Call .start() from a tap (iOS permission rules): jsCopy

The relay has no authentication. Anyone on the same network who knows the room name can join as a controller and move your params. For a show, use a closed network or a room name nobody will guess. On the public relay the room is random and lives in the QR code; it is a convenience for trying a show, not a lock.

Signals are the single currency of the input layer: named, normalized, source-blind. This page lists every signal published by the built-in input packages. Conventions: ranges are 0..1 unless noted pulse signals fire events; their value is the event payload y axes are flipped where it makes performance sense (1 = raised), never raw pixels <n> is a number, <ch> a MIDI channel 1..16, <id> a device id, <slug> a device name made URL-safe

Every hardware message publishes the legacy names and the per-channel names. signalkindrangemeaning midi/note/onpulse{note, vel, velocity, ch, device}key down: vel 0..1, velocity 1..127, ch 1..16, device = port slug midi/note/offpulse{note, ch, device}key up midi/cc/<n>continuous0..1controller n (any channel) midi/bendcontinuous-1..1pitch bend (any channel) midi/ch/<ch>/cc/<n>continuous0..1controller n on one channel midi/ch/<ch>/note/<n>continuous0..1velocity while note n is held, 0 on release midi/ch/<ch>/bendcontinuous-1..1pitch bend on one channel midi/ch/<ch>/pressurecontinuous0..1channel aftertouch midi/ch/<ch>/poly/<n>continuous0..1polyphonic aftertouch on note n With two or more MIDI inputs connected, each device also publishes under its slug (from the port name: Arturia MiniLab 3 → arturia-minilab-3, duplicates get -2, -3): signalkindrangemeaning midi/<slug>/note/onpulse{note, vel, ch}key down on that device midi/<slug>/note/offpulse{note, ch}key up on that device midi/<slug>/cc/<n>continuous0..1controller n on that device midi/<slug>/bendcontinuous-1..1pitch bend on that device On-screen controllers (modules.midi.controllers) publish one name per control, midi/<device>/<control> (for example midi/minilab3/knob1), plus /hit pulses for pads and /raw values. They are listed in MIDI controllers & embedding.

L2 mapping · values over time, the way TouchDesigner's CHOPs shape them: Lag, Trigger (envelope), Speed, Spring, Trail, Slope, Count. Pure logic, no clock of its own: every step is told the seconds that went by and is solved exactly over them, so 30 fps and 144 fps draw the same curve. What the parameters mean follows Derivative's TouchDesigner documentation; the code is OAV's own. In a p5 sketch, oav-p5 gives these one call each: p5 one line. exportsignature approachapproach(current, target, seconds, dt) → one step of a one-pole lag; seconds = time to 63% of a change (the smooth of @openav/mapping, which steps with it) Lagnew Lag({ up = 0.1, down = up }) · step(input, dt, up?, down?) → output · reset(v?): up while rising, down while falling (Lag CHOP's Lag 1 / Lag 2), in TouchDesigner's seconds (about 90% of a change) envelopeenvelope(times, t, attack = 0.01, decay = 0.3, peak = 1) → the Trigger CHOP's level at t for events at times (seconds, oldest first): a straight attack (0 → peak), then 0 after exactly decay; a retrigger starts where it is · envelopeStage(elapsed, attack, decay, from, peak) Speednew Speed() · step(rate, dt) → position: rate per second Springnew Spring({ stiffness = 100, damping = 6 }) · step(target, dt) → position (velocity alongside): a mass on a spring pulled to the input, solved exactly · springStep(x, v, target, k, c, dt) → [x, v] Trailnew Trail({ seconds = 2, rate = 60 }) · step(value, dt) → the last seconds, 60 values a second plus the newest, oldest first, fixed length Slopenew Slope() · step(value, dt) → change per second Countnew Count({ threshold = 0.5 }) · step(on, limit = 0) → times it turned on, looped to 0 … limit − 1 with a limit · wrapCount(total, limit) TD_LAG_RATIO, DEFAULTSMath.LN10: two kinds of seconds. Lag and lag() take TouchDesigner's Lag CHOP seconds (about the time to follow 90% of a change), so lag(x, 0.1) moves like a Lag CHOP set to 0.1; underneath, Lag divides by TD_LAG_RATIO (2.3) to get its time constant. approach(…, seconds) takes that time constant itself (63% of a change, what @openav/mapping's smooth always meant); the defaults above jsCopy

Worlds are visual code, and coding agents are good at code. A person describes a performance ("a jellyfish world that blooms on consonant chords"); an agent writes the world inside a chassis that already handles MIDI, mapping, timeline, console and backstage. This chapter is what an agent needs to do that well.

Continuous control goes through params; discrete events may use signals. Never read signals.get(…) in update() for something that varies continuously. Declare a param and let a route connect the signal to it. The shell never knows the work. Never edit packages/* to make one example look right. A framework change must make every work better. The reasoning is in Core concepts.

AGENTS.md at the repository root is the briefing: what the framework is, the two rules, how to create a new work, how to verify changes, and the conventions (vanilla ESM + JSDoc, no build step, no runtime dependencies, comments that explain the performance reasoning (why a knob feels right) rather than syntax, path-style signal names declared with signals.define).

The repository ships a Model Context Protocol server: packages/mcp/server.js, zero dependencies, JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, one JSON message per line. Claude Code picks it up from .mcp.json when you open the repository. Other clients: jsonCopy It answers initialize (server openav 0.1.0, echoing the client's protocol version, 2024-11-05 if none is given), tools/list and tools/call. Results come back as one text item; objects are JSON-encoded. A failing call returns a JSON-RPC error with code −32000 and a message. toolargumentsreturns list_examplesnone[{ dir, title, summary }]: each example's folder, the <title> of its index.html, and the first comment line of its main.js read_docdoc (required): architecture, writing-a-world, signals, show-control, roadmap, agents, readmethe Markdown text. agents is AGENTS.md, readme the README; the others are docs/<name>.md scaffold_worldslug (required, kebab-case), donor (default 01-hello-particles){ created, next_steps }. This handbook is plain HTML at /docs/ (and /zh/docs/ in Traditional Chinese); every word is there without JavaScript. Each section has a stable anchor, for example /docs/#mapping-curves.

Every show made with createShow() sets window.openav to the whole show, so an agent driving a browser can inspect and steer it: jsCopy

npm test passes (or run_checks says ok). The example loads with zero console errors. The refused ws://…:7457 connection (no backstage monitor running) is expected. It reacts to the on-screen piano or QWERTY keys: no hardware required. Space plays the timeline and something evolves. Report the URL, the params (what to map to knobs), the scenes, and the signals the world listens to.

cheyuwu-lab runs sketches in plain <script> pages, so it builds a classic-script bundle of each OAV package it wants.
